passage:
Thursday, 10:40 pm
Almost did something dumb today.
At six a text said my bank account would be blocked tonight unless I updated my KYC through a link. The sender looked like the bank's name, but one letter was off. My thumb was right over the link.
I made myself do the boring thing: closed the message, opened the bank's own app, logged in normally. No alerts. No pending KYC.
An hour later someone called, very polite, "from the bank", saying an OTP had come to my phone and I should read it out to stop the block. I said, "Banks never ask for OTPs. I'll call the number on my card." He hung up before I finished.
I called the real number and reported both. At dinner I told Leela, and she forwarded my screenshot to her parents.
Note to self: urgency is the hook. Slow is safe.
Saurabh

qa.q: What was off about the sender's name?
qa.a: The sender looked like the bank's name, but one letter was off.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel with a thumb right over the link?
qa.a: Saurabh felt the pull of panic about the block tonight and nearly acted before thinking.

qa.q: Which step protected Saurabh most?
qa.a: Opening the bank's own app directly instead of the link, refusing to read out the OTP, and calling the number on the card to report both.

qa.q: How might Leela's parents benefit from the screenshot?
qa.a: They get a clear example of the fake message before it reaches them, so they are less likely to be rushed into clicking.

grounding: A person checks the sender, opens the bank's official app directly, refuses to share an OTP and reports the fake messages.

passage:
In the small market town, Pradeep ran a stationery shop, and neighbours often brought him their phone troubles. On Tuesday, Yusuf from the tailor's shop came in with an SMS on his phone.
"Your bank account KYC expired. Account will be blocked in 24 hours. Click link to update."
Pradeep put on his glasses and read it slowly. The sender was an ordinary ten-digit number. The link had the bank's name spelt wrong.
"Yusuf bhai, don't click this."
"But what if they block my account?"
"Then we'll open the bank's own app and see." Pradeep opened the official app on Yusuf's phone, the one the bank had installed for him. No KYC warning. Everything normal.
"Real banks don't send links like this. And never share an OTP with anyone. Not even if they say they're from the bank."
Yusuf let out a breath and deleted the message. Pradeep reported the number before the next customer came in.

qa.q: What was wrong with the link in the SMS?
qa.a: The link had the bank's name spelt wrong.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling as he read the SMS slowly?
qa.a: Pradeep felt calm but suspicious, noticing the ordinary number and the misspelt link.

qa.q: What did Pradeep do before clicking anything?
qa.a: He checked the sender, noticed the misspelt link, opened the bank's official app directly, reminded Yusuf never to share an OTP, and reported the number.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel after checking the app?
qa.a: Yusuf felt relieved, letting out a breath and deleting the message.

grounding: It shows an adult checking the sender, refusing to click, opening the official bank app directly and warning never to share an OTP.

passage:
In their small flat in Berlin, Leila was cooking when her phone rang. "Frau Haddad? This is your bank's security team. There's a suspicious payment on your account. We've sent you a code. Please read it to me so we can cancel the transfer."
Leila stopped stirring. Ulla, her flatmate, looked up from the table.
The code arrived by SMS: a six-digit number, with a line underneath: "Never share this code with anyone, including bank staff."
"I'll call you back on the number on my card," Leila said.
"There's no time, madam. The money will be gone."
She hung up.
Her hands were a little unsteady, but she opened the bank's official app herself. No suspicious payment. Then she called the number printed on the back of her card. The real bank confirmed: they never ask customers for codes.
Ulla whistled. "I would have read it out."
"Nearly did," Leila admitted.

qa.q: What did the line under the SMS code say?
qa.a: "Never share this code with anyone, including bank staff."

qa.q: How did Leila feel after hanging up?
qa.a: Leila felt shaken, her hands a little unsteady, but also sure she had done the right thing.

qa.q: What steps did Leila take to check?
qa.a: She refused to read the code, hung up, opened the bank's official app herself, and called the number on the back of her card.

qa.q: How did Ulla react to what happened?
qa.a: Ulla was impressed and a bit alarmed, admitting she would have read the code out.

grounding: It shows an adult refusing to share a one-time code, hanging up and checking through the official app and card number.

passage:
At the insurance office, Tushar opened an email at 5:55 on a Friday evening: "IT Department: your password expires today. Click to keep your account active." The logo looked right.
He almost clicked. Then he stopped and looked at the sender: it-support@ followed by a strange domain, not their company's.
"Manoj, did you get this?"
Manoj, at the next desk, was already hovering over the link. "Yeah, I was just going to update it."
"Don't. Look at the address."
Manoj leaned in. "Oh."
Tushar didn't click. He opened the company's real IT portal from the bookmark he always used. No password warning. He forwarded the email to the real IT helpdesk address and marked it as phishing.
Five minutes later, IT sent a message to the whole office: "Please ignore the password expiry email. It is a phishing attempt."
Manoj bumped his shoulder. "You just saved me a very bad Monday."

qa.q: What was strange about the sender's address?
qa.a: It had a strange domain, not their company's.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel when Tushar pointed out the address?
qa.a: Manoj felt surprised and relieved, realising he had almost clicked the link.

qa.q: What did Tushar do instead of clicking?
qa.a: He checked the sender, opened the real IT portal from his own bookmark, and forwarded the email to the real IT helpdesk as phishing.

qa.q: How did the IT team respond?
qa.a: The IT team warned the whole office within minutes to ignore the fake email.

grounding: It shows an adult checking a sender, not clicking the link, and opening the official portal directly before reporting the phishing email.

passage:
Hi Yusuf,
You asked last week how I always know when a message is fake. I don't! I just slow down. Here's what happened on Monday.
At 7 a.m. I got a text: "Your bank account will be blocked today. Update KYC here," with a link. Then a call from a polite man who said he was from my bank and needed the OTP I'd just received "to stop the block".
I didn't click and I didn't share the OTP. I told him I'd call the bank myself and hung up. Then I checked the sender: a mobile number, not the bank's name. I opened the bank's own app, the one already on my phone, and there was no alert. I called the number printed on my debit card. They said the account was fine, and that no one from the bank would ever ask me for an OTP.
My heart was racing the whole time, by the way. Slowing down doesn't mean feeling calm.
See you Sunday,
Irawati

qa.q: What did the caller ask Irawati for?
qa.a: The OTP just received, to stop the block.

qa.q: How was Irawati feeling while checking?
qa.a: Irawati's heart was racing; Irawati felt anxious even while acting slowly and carefully.

qa.q: Which of Irawati's steps would you advise anyone to copy?
qa.a: Don't click or share the OTP, check the sender, open the bank's own app, and call the number printed on the card.

qa.q: What might Yusuf take from the email?
qa.a: Yusuf may feel reassured that careful people also feel scared, and that a few simple checks matter more than feeling calm.

grounding: Shows a person checking the sender, refusing to click or share an OTP, and contacting the bank directly, which confirms banks never ask for an OTP.
